activities.anchor: money today can be put to work and earn money
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the promise discounted
activities.name: ciTimePredict

config.q: At 8%, £100 in hand becomes £108 in a year. What is a promise of £100 next year worth today?
config.why: The promise discounts back to less than £100 because the cash in hand can grow in the meantime — every loan, bond, mortgage and pension is an application of that one sentence.

activities.anchor: It is the most important mechanism in personal finance
activities.caption: drag the divider — the line vs the curve
activities.name: ciCurveCompare

config.prompt: The same rate, two maths — drag the divider:

before.label: Simple interest
before.text: The same pounds every year on the original principal — a straight line forever, because the earnings are implicitly spent.

after.label: Compounded
after.text: Each year's base is bigger than the last — a curve that steepens without limit. And it cuts both ways: debts compound exactly as enthusiastically as savings.

config.why: Over 40 years at 8%, £10,000 grows to about £217,000 compounded but only £42,000 with simple interest — the reinvestment alone is worth five times the original deposit.

activities.anchor: the difference is why a mortgage's small print is worth reading
activities.caption: call the effective rate — the small print
activities.name: ciEffectiveEstimate

config.prompt: A bank quotes 12% nominal, paid monthly. What effective annual rate does the compounding deliver?
config.why: (1.01)¹² ≈ 12.68% — the gap between quoted and effective grows with both the rate and the frequency, which is exactly where card issuers and payday lenders place their quotes.

activities.caption: line up the doubling times, fastest to slowest
activities.name: ciRuleOrder

config.prompt: Rule of 72 — order the doubling times, fastest first:
config.why: Divide 72 by the annual percentage rate — and the rule runs the other way on debt: paying only the minimum can take decades and cost multiples of the original debt, because most of each minimum payment is new interest.

activities.anchor: A worked example shows how violently distant cash flows shrink
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the discounting memo
activities.name: ciDiscountSpot

config.prompt: One line of this discounting memo is wrong — click it:
lines: A promise of £1,000 in five years is worth about £783 today at a 5% discount rate.
At 10% the same promise shrinks to £621.
Stretch it to thirty years and the value shrinks toward zero (£231 at 5%, £57 at 10%).
The longer the wait, the less the value responds to the rate.
Rising rates lower the present value of everything already promised.
config.correction: The longer the wait, the MORE rate-sensitive the value — distant money swings hardest, which is why long-maturity bonds fall hardest when rates rise.
config.why: Discounting is compounding's mirror: each distant payment shrinks by the growth factor raised to its waiting time, so the rate bites hardest where the waiting is longest.

activities.anchor: Expected value also explains why expected returns must beat the risk-free rate
activities.caption: file the payoff structures
activities.name: ciSkewBuckets

config.prompt: Skewed payoffs, probability-weighted — which businesses run on that structure?

items.label: venture capital — one +50% pays for the frequent small losses
insurance — premiums in, occasional large payouts out
lottery pricing — the same logic in both directions
a government bond's coupon, paid on schedule

config.why: The occasional large gain paying for frequent small losses is the entire logic of those industries — and it is why an 8% expected return on shares exists precisely because the distribution includes bad years a government bond does not.

activities.anchor: market has about one year in six
activities.caption: pin the band — risk as width
activities.name: ciBandPlace

config.prompt: A market with a 10% mean and 16% standard deviation: where does the lower edge of its one-standard-deviation band sit on the annual-return scale?
config.why: One SD below the 10% mean is −6%: about a sixth of years land outside −6% to +26%, and the 95% range spans roughly −22% to +42% — risk is the width of the annual experience, not the sign of the average.

activities.caption: pair each line with its number
activities.name: ciAmortMatch

config.prompt: The compound-interest curve pointed both ways — pair each line with its number:

pairs.left: Month-one interest on a £200,000 mortgage at 6%

config.why: Early payments are mostly interest because the balance being compounded against you is largest — overpaying early removes years from the tail; the annuity runs the same mathematics in reverse, and the infinite stream still sums to a finite number.
